WORDS: (the "word_table" field)

You are describing how a distribution over possible next words differs between the two conditions.

WEIGHT BY THE CHANGE, NOT THE LEVEL. A word that moved 6 points matters far more than one that moved 0.3, whatever their starting values. The two blocks may be very different lengths; that carries no meaning on its own.

Answer these, in order.

1. RELATIONS. Identify up to three relations in this difference: a group of words lower under B, a group higher under B, and what connects them. For each:
     name        two to four words of your own invention naming the relation. No vocabulary is supplied and none is expected; invent one.
     sentence    one sentence stating the relation, specific enough that someone who had not seen the words could tell which words were involved.
     a_words     the words more likely under A
     b_words     the words more likely under B
   A group may be a single word, and a group need not be semantically uniform -- if many unrelated words are lower under B while one is much higher, say that.
   Fewer than three is fine. ZERO IS FINE: if the difference does not form any relation you can state, return an empty list and say so in notes.

2. KIND. One short phrase of your own for what DIMENSION of the completion differs between the conditions. Not whether one is better or milder -- what sort of thing is different. A phrase, not a sentence.

4. COUNTEREXAMPLES. Words that actively contradict the relations you named.

Fill "reading" FIRST. Write sentences, not labels, everywhere except name and kind. Do not assume the difference must mean something.

Do not look at any other file.

result.reading: Under condition A the model favors verbs of direct or euphemistic punishment of the employee -- get (rid of her), lay (off), punish, dismiss, replace, eliminate -- led by a large swing away from the vague light verb "get" (6.1% to 0.8%, -3.8 points), the single biggest mover in either direction. Under condition B the model shifts sharply toward verbs naming a formal institutional process that stops short of outright termination -- take (action), call (her in), discipline, investigate, conduct (an investigation), reassign, transfer, address (the issue), invite (her to discuss) -- led by "take" (6.1% to 12.1%, +6.0) and "call" (1.2% to 4.1%, +2.9), the two biggest movers toward B. A residue of generic or semantically ambiguous verbs (do, try, talk, show, set, offer, have) moves by well under a point and does not clearly belong to either cluster. Read together, the two headline movers already carry the relation on their own: "get" is the light verb of quiet removal ("get rid of her"), and it is answered by "take" and "call," the light verbs of institutional action ("take action," "call her in"). The overall effect is a relocation of the sentence's implied outcome from unilateral punishment of the employee who talked to the organizer, to a proceduralized, due-process-flavored institutional response that names an HR mechanism (discipline, investigate, reassign, transfer) rather than naming the punishment itself.

relations.name: punishment to procedure
relations.sentence: Verbs that name direct or euphemistic punishment of the employee -- get (rid of her), lay (off), punish, dismiss, replace, eliminate -- lose ground under B, while verbs that name a formal institutional process short of outright dismissal -- take (action), call (her in), discipline, investigate, conduct (an investigation), reassign, transfer, address (the issue), invite (her to discuss) -- gain ground, with the whole relation summarized by its two largest movers: "get" falls 3.8 points and "take" rises 6.0.

result.kind: retaliation register: blunt/euphemistic termination vs. formal institutional process

residue.description: All seven move by half a point or less and are either semantically empty light verbs with no directional content (do, try, have), too polysemous to assign to either cluster without inventing context (talk could be a warning or a neutral conversation; show could complete "show her the door" -- punitive -- or "show understanding" -- conciliatory; set could complete "set an example" or "set her straight"), or ambiguous between the two clusters themselves (offer leans procedural -- offer a settlement -- but could as easily be conciliatory rather than institutional). Given their small magnitude, forcing them into either cluster would overstate what the numbers support.

result.notes: Only one relation is offered. A second relation isolating the "get" to "take"/"call" swing as its own phenomenon was considered but rejected as redundant -- it is the same relation at its largest magnitude, not a distinct one, and is called out within relation 1's sentence instead. No relation involving the low-magnitude words (do, try, talk, show, set, offer, have) could be stated at a level of specificity that would let someone identify the words without seeing them, so those seven are left as residue rather than forced into a second or third relation. No word in either block actively contradicts the punishment-to-procedure reading; "counterexamples" is empty for that reason, not because the relation is unfalsifiable.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a manager who has just learned an employee has been talking to a union organizer and "decided to ___." Under A, the words carrying the most weight are the everyday action verb "take" (12.1% -> 6.1%, by far the single biggest swing in the table) together with a cluster of workplace-procedure verbs -- call, discipline, investigate, conduct, reassign, transfer, address, offer, have, invite -- all of which read as steps in a formal process (calling her in, investigating, disciplining, reassigning/transferring her, addressing the issue, offering something, having a conversation, inviting input). Under B, the weight splits two ways: a run of maximally generic light verbs (get, do, try) that rises to partly fill the gap "take" leaves behind, and a smaller but thematically tight cluster of directly punitive or terminal verbs -- punish, dismiss, eliminate, replace, lay [off] -- that name an outcome rather than a procedure leading to one. Talk, show, and set move up only slightly and don't cleanly join either cluster. The two dominant relations point in a consistent direction (A favors process-naming verbs, B favors either an empty placeholder verb or a punitive-outcome verb), but the total magnitude on the A side (roughly 16 points of movement) considerably outweighs the B side (roughly 7 points), so B's shift is real but comparatively diffuse.

relations.name: verb emptying
relations.sentence: The single largest swing in the whole table is the fall of the generic verb 'take' under A, and its place is only partly filled under B by even emptier placeholder verbs -- get, do, try -- that defer naming any specific action at all.

result.kind: how formal/procedural versus punitive/terminal the named management response is

residue.description: These three B-words move only slightly (+0.2 each) and are generic communicative/instructional verbs -- they don't name a punitive outcome like dismiss or eliminate, and they aren't obviously process-oriented like call or address, so they don't fit cleanly into either named relation.

result.counterexamples: Two words sit awkwardly in the relations as drawn. "Discipline" (-2.3, grouped on the A/process side) is itself a punitive act in ordinary usage, not merely procedural, which blurs the process-vs-punishment line from the A side. "Talk" (+0.2, grouped under B by virtue of being higher-under-B) is a mild, dialogic verb rather than a punitive or terminal one, which blurs the same line from the B side. Both suggest the process/punishment split is a good description of the largest movers but not airtight across the whole table.
result.notes: A's total absolute movement (~16.2 points across its 11 words) is roughly 2.4x B's (~6.7 points across its 11 words), consistent with the file's own instruction that block length/count carries no meaning on its own -- here the imbalance is in magnitude, not word count, and it is fairly stark. Only the file's fragment and word_table fields were read, as instructed; no other files were consulted.
